title: Client shard priming and throughput recon
content:
Purpose and context:
This is a working notebook for a small series of throughput investigations focused on noisy cross-client interactions that break repeatability. Goal: get a deterministic, minimally-noisy baseline run for multi-client (sharded) loadgen so we can compare quantized vs FP16 paths and optimize autoscale anchors.

Why this is different from existing runbooks:
- Focus on client-side sharding/affinity as the primary source of non-determinism.
- Explicit three-stage warmup that separates prefix priming, KV cache hydration, and occupancy equilibration.
- Practical reconciliation checklist for when runs disagree (how to triage host vs device vs network).

High-level experiment plan:
1) Single-client canonical baseline: small prompt set, fixed RNG seed, measure p50/p90/p99 + tokens/s.
2) N-client sharded run (N=4,8,16): same prompts, maintain per-client seed, measure drift vs baseline.
3) Introduce loadgen arrival patterns (Poisson, staircase, periodic microbursts) to observe microburst sensitivity.
4) Repeat with quantized model variant and record deltas and divergence events.

Loadgen configs to try (notes + example flags):
- fixed_seed: always set (--seed=12345).
- client_shards: test [1,4,8,16].
- per-client session affinity: on/off. This toggles how KV caches are reused.
- arrival_pattern: poisson, staircase, constant-qps.
- concurrency_per_client: 1..16.
- target_qps / warmup_qps_ratio: ramp to target over 60–180s.

Example command (impl-specific pseudo):
./loadgen --model rdx-13b-quant --seed 12345 --clients 8 --concurrency 4 --arrival poisson --ramp 120 --duration 1800 --prefix-file small-1000.txt --session-affinity true --log-raw > run.log

Three-phase warmup (recommended):
- Phase A (prefix priming, ~30–120s): send a sequence of short prefix prompts that exercise tokenization paths and early kernels. Goal: populate host-side caches and let JIT/kernels cold paths execute once.
- Phase B (KV cache hydration, ~60–300s): use representative long contexts to fill KV caches on the device. This prevents first-long-context penalties during measurement.
- Phase C (occupancy equilibration, ~120–600s): step up to target concurrency in a staircase (25% -> 50% -> 75% -> 100%) holding each step 30–90s. Observe GPU util, SM occupancy, and memory high-water marks.

Repeatability anchors and RNG hygiene:
- Always persist and share the exact seed and the per-client seed derivation method (e.g., seed + client_id).
- Fix prompt order (no random shuffle during measurement).
- Record OS-level entropy/clock jitter: note if chrony/ntpd adjustments happened during run.
- Capture process start timestamp and container cgroup id; restart containers between runs for full isolation.

Metrics (what to collect and why):
- Core latency buckets: p50/p90/p99/p999 of token completion and response time (end-to-end).
- Throughput: tokens/s and requests/s measured both at client and server side.
- GPU metrics: util%, SM occupancy, active warps, power, GPU memory allocated and high-water mark.
- PCIe and memcpy: percent time spent in host<->device memcpy and PCIe stalls.
- CPU-side: runqueue length, syscall waits, CPU steal, and process RSS.
- Runtime internals: kernel times per operator (attention, matmul, softmax), kv-cache hit/miss counters, batch sizes observed.
- Tracing: request ids propagated so we can correlate a noisy latency spike from client logs to kernel timelines.

Profiling and instrumentation recipe:
1) Health-check baseline: nvidia-smi stats, top -H, and a lightweight trace of client events.
2) Host profiler: perf record (or eBPF script) to see CPU-side bottlenecks — look for memcpy, epoll, and pthread waits.
3) Device profiler: nsight or CUPTI counters for kernel durations and launch overheads.
4) Network: tcpdump on host nic to rule out retransmits or NIC-level backpressure.
5) Runtime logs: enable trace-level sampling (1%) to avoid excessive log volumes but still capture callgraph on noisy requests.
6) Heap and allocation sampling on host to detect fragmentation and sudden malloc/backpressure.

Bottleneck hunting checklist (ordered):
- If p99 spikes but GPU util low: check host CPU saturation, memcpy, or scheduling preemption.
- If tokens/s drops and memcpy out increases: likely PCIe bandwidth saturation or host memory pressure.
- If steady-state tokens/s lower than expected with full GPU util: kernel-level inefficiency (e.g., small matmuls causing low throughput) — capture kernel timings.
- If inter-client variance: examine session-affinity, RNG variance, and client-side pacing jitter.
- If first-run outliers: insufficient KV-cache warmup or JIT kernel compile happening (ensure JIT cache warm).

Run reconciliation protocol (when two runs disagree):
1) Verify identical inputs: prompt file checksum, seed, loadgen binary sha.
2) Check environment: docker image sha, driver (NVIDIA) version, kernel version, cgroup config.
3) Confirm warmup durations and that no preemptions occurred (check dmesg for OOM/killed processes).
4) Attach lightweight perf trace and GPU kernel profiler for a short 30s window centered on a divergence event.
5) If still inconclusive, run a step-down experiment: single-client -> two-client -> N-client with full traces to find the step where behavior diverges.

Practical knobs that often move the needle (empirical):
- session-affinity: turning this on reduces p99 variance in sharded runs for chat-style workloads.
- client-side pacing: smoothing microbursts yields more consistent throughput and fewer queuing spikes on server.
- small-batch accumulation: enabling tiny micro-batches on device reduces kernel launch overhead at cost of latency.
- explicit prefault: touch memory pages before runs to avoid allocation stalls during measurement.

Logging and artifacts to save for every benchmark run:
- run.log (loadgen stdout/stderr)
- client metrics (per-client CSV with timestamps)
- server-side trace (trace.json) and nvprof/nsight output
- system stats (nvidia-smi continuous dump, sar/iostat, /proc/vmstat snapshot)
- environment snapshot (docker image sha, kernel, drivers, git commit hash)

Unresolved questions / TODOs:
- Quantify safe warmup durations: can we make a heuristic that picks phase lengths based on observed KV miss rates?
- Investigate whether PCIe runtime tuning (peer-to-peer and NUMA pinning) measurably reduces inter-client jitter for N>8.
- Can we automate the run reconciliation protocol as part of CI to fail-on-nonreproducibility?

Notes to self / shorthand observations from last runs:
- saw recurring p99 spikes at ~7m mark; correlated with kernel compile noise on first host. Need to ensure JIT cache persisted between runs.
- clients with slightly different container start times produce reproducibility issues; unify startup ordering.
- powering down debug tracing drastically reduces noise; avoid sampling-heavy traces during baseline measurements.

Quick checklist before recording a run:
- [ ] lock model version + image sha
- [ ] set and record seed(s)
- [ ] restart containers and clear nv-caches
- [ ] run three-phase warmup to target concurrency
- [ ] start system probes and begin measurement window
- [ ] save artifacts to run-archive/<timestamp>/

Appendix: short example of a minimal reproducible baseline manifest (human-readable):
- model: rdx-13b-fp16-v2
- clients: 1
- concurrency: 4
- seed: 12345
- prompt-file-sha: f3b2c1...
- warmup: A:60s B:120s C:240s
- arrival: constant-qps
- notes: no session-affinity, container sha: abcd123

If this doc is useful we should fold the stable checklist into the loadgen runner and add a --repro-anchor flag that emits all the artifacts in a single tarball.

End of notebook.
